ideas.title: Writing

date.marks: The earliest proto-cuneiform tablets (Uruk IV phase)
date.note: 3200 BCE is a conventional date. Almost all of the earliest tablets were found in rubbish deposits that cannot be dated precisely [@woods-2010-mesopotamia, p. 34]. Writing appeared at roughly the same time in Egypt [@woods-2010-intro, p. 15].

ideas.summary: Administrators in Uruk, arguably the world's first city, begin recording goods and labour on clay tablets. Writing starts as a tool of bureaucracy, not literature, and is invented independently at least four times: in Mesopotamia, Egypt, China and Mesoamerica.
ideas.body:
**The first city.** In the Late Uruk period (c. 3350–3100 BCE), Uruk grew to 20,000–50,000 people and became "arguably, the world's first true city." The new administration needed to track production, goods and labour, and writing was invented in that setting [@woods-2010-mesopotamia, p. 34].

**Precursors.** Before writing, Near Eastern administrators kept accounts with small clay tokens, some sealed inside clay envelopes ("bullae"). That the tokens were forerunners of the earliest tablets, first argued by Denise Schmandt-Besserat, is "core knowledge" among cuneiformists. Many of the numerical signs on early tablets match the tokens in form and function [@englund-2004, p. 100].

**Dating.** The earliest tablets fall into two script phases: Uruk IV (c. 3200 BCE) and Uruk III (c. 3100 BCE). The German Archaeological Institute excavated about 5,000 proto-cuneiform tablets at Uruk between 1928 and 1976 [@woods-2010-mesopotamia, p. 35]. The whole proto-cuneiform corpus runs to over 6,000 tablets and fragments [@englund-2004, p. 100].

**Purpose.** Nearly all the earliest texts are administrative. Literature, religious texts, historical documents and letters appear only from the mid-third millennium BCE, some 700 years after the first written evidence [@woods-2010-mesopotamia, p. 34].

**Independent inventions.** There are four "pristine" writing systems, invented with no knowledge of writing elsewhere: Mesopotamia and Egypt at the end of the fourth millennium BCE, China at the end of the second millennium BCE, and Mesoamerica by the middle of the first millennium BCE [@woods-2010-intro, p. 15].

ideas.title: Royal sun temples of the Fifth Dynasty

date.marks: Approximate start of Userkaf's reign, the first king credited with building a sun temple; the temple's construction date itself is not fixed.
date.note: Old Kingdom absolute dates vary by chronology. Magli and Bárta (via Archaeology magazine) give Userkaf's reign as about 2465–2458 BCE [@magli-2009, PDF p. 6; @archaeology-sun-kings-2020, founder paragraph], while UCL's Digital Egypt dates the dynasty to 2450–2300 BCE [@ucl-digital-egypt-userkaf, entry text].

ideas.origin: Userkaf, Fifth Dynasty Egypt (Abu Ghurab, near Abusir)
ideas.summary: Userkaf, founder of Egypt's Fifth Dynasty, is credited as the first king to build a sun temple to Ra, at Abu Ghurab, in addition to his pyramid. How many later kings did the same is debated.
ideas.body:
Userkaf, first king of the Fifth Dynasty, is described by UCL's Digital Egypt as "the first king who built a sun temple to support his eternal cult". His temple at Abu Ghurab, called Nekhen-Re, is known from excavation reports by Ricke and Edel [@ucl-digital-egypt-userkaf, entry text]. Besides it, he was buried in a pyramid at Saqqara [@ucl-digital-egypt-userkaf, entry text]. The idea is therefore a second royal monument, devoted to the sun god, built beside the pyramid. Magli also calls Userkaf's the first sun temple in the Abu Gorab zone. He describes a lower building and an access ramp leading up to a monumental area, where a stone base carried a high, non-monolithic obelisk. He suggests the plan was probably a copy of the temple at Heliopolis [@magli-2009, PDF p. 6].

Scholars read the purpose in different ways. Miroslav Bárta, in a magazine interview, says the Fifth Dynasty temples were dedicated to Ra and linked the pharaoh's authority to the sun god's supremacy [@archaeology-sun-kings-2020, founder paragraph]. He adds that offerings for royal mortuary complexes were first taken to the temples to be exposed to the sun before going on to the mortuary temples [@archaeology-sun-kings-2020, six-temples paragraph]. Magli proposes instead that such temples signalled the king's link with the sun god when his pyramid's location did not already show it [@magli-2009, PDF p. 11]. This second reading is a hypothesis and not a settled view.

The number of temples is disputed. Bárta's account gives six sun temples in the dynasty [@archaeology-sun-kings-2020, six-temples paragraph]. Magli notes that texts of the period suggest Sahure, Neferefre, Neferirkare and Menkauhor also built them, but these temples have never been found. Some scholars (citing Verner 2002 and Nuzzolo 2007) hold that those texts refer to renewals of Userkaf's temple, so that Niuserre's was the only other temple actually built. Magli himself argues that the missing temples never existed [@magli-2009, PDF pp. 10–11]. The firm archaeological evidence is therefore for two temples, Userkaf's and Niuserre's. Dates for both are approximate.

ideas.title: The Alphabet

date.marks: The earliest known alphabetic inscriptions, from Egypt and Sinai
date.note: The earliest alphabetic inscriptions lack stratified archaeological contexts, so their dates are uncertain [@lam-2010, p. 189]. The 22-letter alphabet associated with the Phoenicians stabilized around 1000 BCE [@lam-2010, p. 192].

ideas.origin: Semitic-speaking workers in Egypt and Sinai; later standardized by the Phoenicians
ideas.summary: Semitic speakers in Egypt borrow hieroglyphic pictures but use each one for a single sound. A few dozen signs can write a whole language. Most of the world's major scripts, from Latin and Cyrillic to Arabic and Devanagari, descend from it.
ideas.body:
**Invention.** The earliest alphabetic inscriptions come from Serabit el-Khadem, an Egyptian mining site in Sinai, and from Wadi el-Hol near Thebes [@lam-2010, p. 189]. The two Wadi el-Hol inscriptions date to roughly 1900–1800 BCE [@herrmann-2023]. "The alphabet was invented among Semitic speakers in the Egyptian realm, inspired iconographically by hieroglyphic writing but not bound by its modes of expression" [@lam-2010, p. 190]. Workers at the Sinai turquoise mines, or Canaanites living in Egypt, are the likeliest inventors [@herrmann-2023].

**How it worked.** Each sign took its sound from the first consonant of the West Semitic word for the thing pictured (the *acrophonic principle*): a hand, *kaph*, stood for /k/ [@lam-2010, pp. 189–190]. Alphabets need tens of signs where logographic and syllabic systems need hundreds. Most of the world's common languages, Chinese and Japanese aside, are written in scripts descended from this linear West Semitic alphabet [@lam-2010, p. 189].

**Development.** Proto-Canaanite inscriptions in the Levant run from the 17th century BCE, and most date from the 13th century or later. Around 1000 BCE the script stabilized as a 22-letter alphabet written right to left, matching the sounds of Phoenician. Hebrew and Aramaic speakers adopted it, and the oldest Greek inscriptions appear in the 8th century BCE [@lam-2010, pp. 191–193].

**A caution about literacy.** It is tempting to say the alphabet put literacy within everyone's reach. Lam argues against this: although it probably made scribal training easier, "no immediate correlation can be made between alphabetic writing and broad literacy" [@lam-2010, p. 189].

ideas.title: Positional Mathematics
ideas.summary: A base-60 place-value system makes large calculations tractable — its echo survives in our 60-minute hours and 360° circles.

ideas.title: Written Law
ideas.summary: Laws carved in public stone: justice as a fixed, knowable standard rather than the whim of a ruler.

ideas.title: Monotheism
ideas.origin: Akhenaten, Egypt; later the Hebrew Bible
ideas.summary: The radical notion of a single, universal god — briefly tried in Egypt, later the foundation of Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

ideas.title: Natural Explanation
ideas.summary: The world can be explained by natural causes rather than the will of gods — the seed of both philosophy and science.

ideas.title: Democracy
ideas.summary: Citizens govern themselves directly by vote. Limited to free men, but the principle of rule by the people is born.

ideas.title: Confucian Ethics
ideas.summary: Social harmony grows from virtue, ritual and right relationships. It would shape Chinese government for two millennia.

ideas.title: Buddhism

date.marks: The death of the Buddha; his teaching career came in the decades before
date.note: Traditional Theravada chronology puts his death in 544/543 BCE; a corrected version gives 487/486 BCE, and the Indian "short chronology" 370–368 BCE [@violatti-2015]. A review of the 1988 Göttingen symposium on the question favoured about 400 BCE [@cousins-1996].

ideas.origin: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha; northern India
ideas.summary: In his first sermon, near Varanasi, the Buddha sets out the Four Noble Truths: suffering arises from craving, and it ends when craving is let go.
ideas.body:
**The teaching.** The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, traditionally the Buddha's first sermon, delivered at Isipatana near Varanasi, identifies the origin of suffering as "the craving that makes for further becoming" and its cessation as "the remainderless fading & cessation, renunciation, relinquishment, release, & letting go of that very craving" [@sn-56-11].

**The dating problem.** The Theravada tradition dates the Buddha's death to 544/543 BCE. Checking it against the reign of the emperor Ashoka produced a corrected date of 487/486 BCE, while Indian sources point to 370–368 BCE. At a 1988 symposium on the question in Göttingen, experts proposed dates ranging from 486 to 261 BCE [@violatti-2015]. Reviewing the published volumes, Cousins concluded that "the evidence seems to favour some kind of median chronology and we should no doubt speak of a date for the Buddha's Mahaparinibbana of c.400 B.C." [@cousins-1996].

ideas.title: The Examined Life
ideas.summary: Truth is pursued by relentless questioning. Executed for it, Socrates makes intellectual inquiry a moral act.

ideas.title: Formal Logic
ideas.summary: The syllogism codifies valid reasoning itself. Aristotle's system would dominate Western and Islamic thought for 2,000 years.

ideas.title: Axiomatic Proof
ideas.summary: From a handful of axioms, all of geometry follows by proof. The template for rigorous knowledge ever since.

ideas.title: Christianity
ideas.summary: A message of universal love and salvation that would become the faith of the Roman Empire and reshape the West.

ideas.title: Paper
ideas.summary: A cheap, light writing surface from plant fibre. It travels the Silk Road and makes books abundant.

ideas.title: Mathematical Astronomy
ideas.summary: An Earth-centred cosmos described with geometric precision — wrong, but predictive enough to reign for 1,400 years.

ideas.title: Islam
ideas.summary: A unifying faith and legal tradition that, within a century, spans from Spain to Central Asia.

ideas.title: Zero as a Number
ideas.summary: Zero gets rules of arithmetic of its own. With Hindu–Arabic numerals, calculation becomes something anyone can do.

ideas.title: Algebra
ideas.summary: Systematic methods for solving equations. His name gives us the word algorithm.

ideas.title: The University
ideas.summary: A self-governing community of scholars. Learning gains an institution independent of monastery and court.

ideas.title: Rule of Law
ideas.summary: Even the king is bound by law. A narrow baronial deal becomes a lasting symbol of limits on power.

ideas.title: The Printing Press
ideas.summary: Movable metal type makes books cheap and identical. Within fifty years, millions are in circulation.

ideas.title: Political Realism
ideas.summary: Politics described as it is, not as it ought to be. Power is analysed on its own terms.

ideas.title: The Reformation
ideas.summary: Individual conscience and scripture over Church authority. Printing spreads the challenge across Europe in weeks.

ideas.title: Heliocentrism
ideas.summary: The Earth moves around the Sun. Humanity is displaced from the centre of the cosmos.

ideas.title: The Scientific Method
ideas.summary: Knowledge built from systematic observation and experiment rather than inherited authority.

ideas.title: Universal Laws of Nature
ideas.summary: The same mathematical laws govern a falling apple and orbiting planets. The universe becomes a knowable machine.

ideas.title: Natural Rights
ideas.summary: People are born with rights to life, liberty and property; government is legitimate only by their consent.

ideas.title: Separation of Powers
ideas.origin: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws
ideas.summary: Liberty is safest when legislative, executive and judicial power check one another.

ideas.title: The Market Economy
ideas.origin: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations
ideas.summary: Self-interest, coordinated by markets and the division of labour, produces collective prosperity.

ideas.title: Universal Rights
ideas.origin: Declaration of the Rights of Man, France
ideas.summary: Rights belong to all people by nature. Revolutions in America and France put Enlightenment ideas into practice.

ideas.title: Women's Rights
ideas.summary: If rights are universal, they belong to women too. An argument that would take centuries to win.

ideas.title: Historical Materialism
ideas.summary: History is a struggle between classes; capitalism will give way to collective ownership. It would move nations.

ideas.title: Evolution by Natural Selection
ideas.origin: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species
ideas.summary: All life descends from common ancestors, shaped by selection over immense time. Humanity joins the animal kingdom.

ideas.title: Individual Liberty
ideas.summary: The only justification for restricting a person's freedom is to prevent harm to others.

ideas.title: Germ Theory

date.marks: Pasteur's campaign against spontaneous generation begins
date.note: Germ theory took shape over several decades rather than at one moment. Key work runs from Semmelweis (1847) to Koch's anthrax paper (1876) and beyond [@cavaillon-2022; @blevins-2010].

ideas.origin: Semmelweis, Pasteur, Davaine, Lister, Koch and others
ideas.summary: Specific diseases are caused by specific living microorganisms. Built up over decades of experiments by many researchers, the idea made antiseptic surgery possible and launched medical bacteriology.
ideas.body:
**Many hands.** Precursors of germ theory go back at least to Girolamo Fracastoro (1546), who thought diseases spread through "seminaria," or seeds [@cavaillon-2022]. The theory's 19th-century foundations were laid by several people:

- **Semmelweis (1847)** showed that medical students' hands, after autopsies, carried infection to women giving birth [@cavaillon-2022].
- **Pasteur (from 1860–61)** took up the Academy of Sciences' challenge to settle the question of spontaneous generation. The decisive swan-neck flask experiments, which showed that the air carries germs, were conceived by his colleague Antoine Balard [@cavaillon-2022].
- **Davaine (1863)** found bacteria in the blood of animals with anthrax and showed that the disease spread through infected blood. Historians credit him with the first demonstration that a bacterium causes disease [@cavaillon-2022].
- **Lister (1865)** learned of Pasteur's theory and applied it to surgery, using phenol as an antiseptic [@cavaillon-2022].
- **Koch (1876)** published his study of the anthrax bacillus [@koch-1876]. This work "launched the field of medical bacteriology" [@blevins-2010].

**Myth and reality.** Cavaillon and Legout write explicitly to separate Pasteur's real achievements from "the legend built by his hagiographers," in part a legend he cultivated himself [@cavaillon-2022]. Crediting the theory to one or two famous names misrepresents how it was built.

ideas.title: The Unconscious Mind
ideas.origin: Sigmund Freud, The Interpretation of Dreams
ideas.summary: Much of what drives us is hidden from ourselves. The self is no longer fully transparent to reason.

ideas.title: Relativity
ideas.summary: Space and time are not absolute but bend with motion and gravity. Mass and energy are interchangeable.

ideas.title: Quantum Mechanics
ideas.summary: At the smallest scales, nature is probabilistic. The clockwork universe gives way to uncertainty.

ideas.title: Universal Computation
ideas.summary: A single abstract machine can perform any computation. The theoretical blueprint for every computer.

ideas.title: Universal Human Rights
ideas.summary: After world war and genocide, the nations of the world affirm rights belonging to every human being.

ideas.title: Information Theory
ideas.summary: Information can be measured in bits and transmitted reliably through noise. The foundation of digital communication.

ideas.title: The Double Helix
ideas.summary: Heredity is written in a molecular code. Life itself becomes legible as information.

ideas.title: Paradigm Shifts
ideas.summary: Science advances not steadily but through revolutions that overturn whole frameworks of thought.

ideas.title: Packet-Switched Networks
ideas.summary: Computers talk to each other by breaking messages into packets. The seed of the internet.

ideas.title: The World Wide Web
ideas.summary: Hyperlinked documents open to anyone. Publishing becomes nearly free, as printing once made copying cheap.

ideas.title: Deep Learning
ideas.summary: Neural networks trained on vast data surpass hand-built systems. Machines learn from examples, not rules.

ideas.title: The Transformer

date.marks: Publication of "Attention Is All You Need"

ideas.origin: Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need"
ideas.summary: A neural network architecture built on attention alone, without recurrence, so it can be trained efficiently in parallel. It became the basis of language models such as BERT (2018) and GPT-3 (2020).
ideas.body:
**The idea.** The paper proposed "a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely." The authors reported that it was "more parallelizable" and required "significantly less time to train" than the recurrent and convolutional models it replaced [@vaswani-2017, abstract].

**What was new.** Attention itself was older. It had already been added to recurrent translation models, letting a model "(soft-)search for parts of a source sentence that are relevant to predicting a target word" [@bahdanau-2014, abstract]. The Transformer's step was to make attention the whole architecture.

**What followed.** BERT, short for "Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers" [@devlin-2018, abstract], was built on it. So was GPT-3, which uses "the same model and architecture as GPT-2" with sparse attention patterns "in the layers of the transformer" [@brown-2020, §2.1].

events.place: Beeches Pit, West Stow, Suffolk, England (UK)
events.summary: At least three distinct burning horizons, including probable hearths and heated artefacts, were identified at Beeches Pit, in a period of fire-use evidence in East Anglia around 400,000 years ago.
events.body:
> At Beeches Pit, 10 km south-west of Barnham, at least three distinct burning horizons, including probable hearths and heated artefacts, have been identified. [@pab-fire-400ka, Barnham section, Implications]

> In Europe there is occasional evidence of fire-use from around 400,000 years ago [@pab-fire-400ka, Background]

events.title: Deposition of PC4 sediments

date.marks: Deposition of PC4 sediments, from the age-depth model (1σ about 35 ka)

events.summary: Sediments of PC4, which host Karatau Culture artefacts, were deposited around 400 ka.
events.body: > sediments of pedocomplexes PC4, PC5, and PC6 associated with the Early Palaeolithic Karatau Culture were deposited around ~400, ~500 ka, and ~580 ka, respectively, with a modelled age uncertainty (1σ) of ~35 ka [@sorensen-2026, Results]

events.title: Earliest Acheulian assemblages in eastern Africa, Kapthurin Levallois blanks by about 400 ka

date.marks: Levallois flake blanks used for LCT production, by ~400 ka

events.summary: Levallois flake blanks were used for LCT production by about 400 ka at sites in the Kapthurin Formation in Kenya.
events.body: > Levallois flake blanks were used for LCT production by ~ 400 ka at sites in the Kapthurin Formation in Kenya [@blackwood-2026-2, Discussion]

events.title: Evidence of fire-making at Barnham, Suffolk

date.marks: Source describes a '400,000-year-old buried landsurface'; the project page also says 'over 400,000 years ago', with deposits laid down in the Hoxnian interglacial (MIS 11).
date.note: Described by the excavators as over 400,000 years old; the year is a round figure, not a measured age.

events.summary: Heated sediments, fire-cracked flint handaxes and two fragments of iron pyrite on a buried land surface at Barnham are interpreted as evidence of fire-making about 400,000 years ago.
events.body: > Here we present evidence of fire-making on a 400,000-year-old buried landsurface at Barnham (UK), where heated sediments and fire-cracked flint handaxes were found alongside two fragments of iron pyrite [@davis-2025, Abstract]

events.title: Fire use at Gruta da Aroeira

date.marks: Early use of fire, around 400 ka, correlated with MIS 11

events.summary: Early use of fire at Gruta da Aroeira is dated around 400 ka, correlated with MIS 11.
events.body:
> New research from the Portuguese site of Gruta da Aroeira also testifies to the early use of fire around 400 ka, correlated with MIS 11 [@kot-2022, Discussion]

> In the Gruta da Aroeira cave site (Portugal), for example, fire proxies in the form of heated bones start to appear in layers dated to 400 ka [@macdonald-2021, The Spatiotemporal Pattern of Fire Use]

events.title: Increase in fire at Lake deep sea core

date.marks: Increase in fire, about 400 000 years ago

events.summary: A deep sea core records an increase in fire about 400 000 years ago, though anthropogenic implications may be absent.
events.body: > A rare study based on elemental carbon in a deep sea core indicates an increase in fire at about 400 000 years ago [@gowlett-2016, 7. The impact of fire]

events.title: Landscape around Olorgesailie becomes more variable about 400,000 years ago

date.marks: Source's own figure 'around 400,000 years ago', from the Koora drill core record; −400,000.

events.summary: A Koora-basin drill core shows the environment of the southern Kenya Rift became more variable around 400,000 years ago, when tectonic activity fragmented the landscape.
events.body: > the environment in this part of Africa became more variable around 400,000 years ago, when tectonic activity fragmented the landscape. [@smithsonian-olorgesailie-2020, News release, 21 Oct 2020]

events.title: Last occurrences of Lycaon lycaonoides around MIS 11

date.marks: Last occurrences of Lycaon lycaonoides, around MIS 11

events.summary: The last occurrences of the giant hunting dog Lycaon lycaonoides are recorded in Hungary and Poland around MIS 11.
events.body: > the last occurrences of this species are recorded in Hungary and Poland around MIS 11 [@kot-2022, Discussion]

events.title: Levallois cores in Acheulean context at Kapthurin Formation, Kenya

date.marks: Tephrochronology, '~ 400 ka', as summarised by White et al. 2024 citing Tryon et al. 2006, Blegen et al. 2018 and Shipton 2022.

events.summary: The earliest known cores conforming fully to the Levallois concept are reported from an Acheulean context in the Kapthurin Formation, dated by tephrochronology to about 400 ka.
events.body: > The earliest known cores that fully conform to Boëda’s Levallois concept are found in an Acheulean context in the Kapthurin Formation, Kenya, dated by tephrochronology to ~ 400 ka [@white-2024, Introduction, 'When Is Levallois Not Levallois?']

events.title: Levallois technique and hafting originate

date.marks: Levallois technique, around 400 000 years ago

events.summary: The Levallois technique originates around 400 000 years ago, giving indications of the beginnings of hafting.
events.body: > The Levallois technique of stone working originates around the same period, and gives strong indications of the beginnings of hafting [@gowlett-2016, 6. Fire origins in the archaeological record]

events.title: Middle Stone Age emergence in East and northeast Africa

date.marks: Onset of the MSA in several instances

events.summary: The Middle Stone Age archaeological category seems to have commenced more than 400 ka in several instances.
events.body: > which as an archaeological category seems to have commenced more than 400 ka in several instances in subequatorial and northeastern Africa [@berger-2017-3, Implications for the archaeological record]

events.title: Shift in precipitation regime after MIS 11

date.marks: Shift in precipitation regime after MIS 11 (around 400 ka), as proposed explanation

events.body: > One explanation for the disappearance of hominins may be linked to a possible shift away from a summer precipitation regime to a winter precipitation regime in Tajikistan after MIS 11 [@sorensen-2026-2, Discussion]

events.title: Acheulian ends and Middle Palaeolithic emerges at Attirampakkam, India

date.marks: Luminescence dating, 385 ± 64 ka; converted to BCE as −385,000 with the stated error as range.
date.note: The Middle Palaeolithic at the site is reported to continue until 172 ± 41 ka.

events.body: > Luminescence dating at the stratified prehistoric site of Attirampakkam, India, has shown that processes signifying the end of the Acheulian culture and the emergence of a Middle Palaeolithic culture occurred at 385 ± 64 thousand years ago (ka) [@akhilesh-2018, Abstract]

events.body: > Trench one preserves two infrared-radiofluorescence (IR-RF) dated levels; upper gravels and sand lenses with dates clustering at approximately 372 ka, while the dates for the lower gravels cluster at about 542 ka (ref. 25 ). [@key-2025-3, Results]

events.title: Homo naledi remains deposited in the Dinaledi Chamber, Rising Star Cave

date.marks: Placed at the older bound of the reported 236–335 ka depositional window (US-ESR on teeth combined with U-Th on the oldest overlying flowstone).
date.note: The wider sediment unit is interpreted as deposited between 236 and 414 ka; a minimum-age scenario for the teeth gives about 200 ka. The authors favour the maximum-age scenario.

events.place: Rising Star Cave (Dinaledi Chamber), South Africa
events.summary: Combined OSL, U-Th, palaeomagnetic and US-ESR dating constrains the deposition of Homo naledi fossils to between 236 and 335 ka.
events.body:

> New ages for flowstone, sediments and fossil bones from the Dinaledi Chamber are presented. [@dirks-2017, Abstract]

events.summary: Nor Geghi 1 has obsidian assemblages with both bifaces and Levallois cores in alluvial layers correlated with OIS 9e (335–325 ka), described as the earliest synchronic use of both technologies outside Africa.

events.body: > The MIS 9 to 7 time-span in Europe, roughly 350,000 to 200,000 B.P., is considered to have recorded a behavioural change commonly described as the shift from the Lower to the Middle Palaeolithic [@carmignani-2017, Introduction]

events.title: Italian fossils dated around 300–250 ka

events.summary: Fragmentary fossils dated to around 300–250 ka, including Casal de' Pazzi and Sedia del Diavolo, still show a mixture of archaic and progressive features.
events.body: > Meanwhile, on the Italian Peninsula the fragmentary collections of fossils dated to around 300–250 ka, such as the parietal bone from Casal de’ Pazzi [@picin-2013, Discussion]

events.title: Middle Stone Age earliest evidence around 300–250 ka

date.marks: Earliest evidence of the African Middle Stone Age

events.summary: The earliest evidence of the Middle Stone Age is found contemporaneously around 300–250 ka across much of the continent.
events.body: > the earliest evidence of which is found contemporaneously around 300–250 ka across much of the continent [@meneganzin-2022-2, Section 2.1]

events.title: Transition to Middle Paleolithic in northwestern Europe and Near East

date.marks: Lower to Middle Paleolithic transition, from Hérisson and Soriano

events.summary: Hérisson and Soriano situate the Lower to Middle Paleolithic transition, marked by full Levallois adoption, between 280 and 250 ka.
events.body: > situate the transition of the Lower to Middle Paleolithic, exemplified by the full adoption of Levallois technology, between 280 and 250 ka, in northwestern Europe as well as in the Near East [@macdonald-2021, Intensified Intergroup Interactions]

events.title: Florisbad hominin material dated to about 260 ka, South Africa

date.marks: Age of the Florisbad craniofacial fragments and molar, from direct dating
date.note: Some scholars have raised doubts on the contemporaneity of the remains and the presence of H. sapiens in southern Africa at 260 ka.

events.summary: Grün and colleagues dated the Florisbad material to ca. 260 ka, a date some scholars question because of stratigraphic doubts.
events.body:
> as a primitive H. sapiens dated to ca. 260 ka [@meneganzin-2022, Section 3.1]

> some to raise doubts on the contemporaneity of such remains and, consequently, on the actual presence of H. sapiens in southern Africa at 260 ka [@meneganzin-2022, Section 3.1]

events.title: Florisbad hominin skull dated (Kalahari Basin context)

date.marks: Florisbad fossil, one of the earliest known H. sapiens clade fossils

events.summary: Florisbad is noted as a site of formal archaeological investigation beginning in the 1930s and 40s.
events.body: > One of the earliest known fossils of the H. sapiens clade was found at Florisbad, [@wilkins-2021, Section 1. Introduction]

events.title: Florisbad Homo sapiens fossil

date.marks: Florisbad human fossils, dated to about 260 ka

events.summary: Human fossils from Florisbad document Homo sapiens in southern Africa, dated to about 260 ka.
events.body:
> Human fossils from Florisbad (~260 ka) 31 and Border Cave (~170–80 ka) 30 document the presence of Homo sapiens in southern Africa during the late Middle Pleistocene. [@will-2026-3, Discussion]

> The earliest H. sapiens fossils are in Africa. [@wilkins-2021, Section 1. Introduction]

> The earliest fossils described as belonging to “the H. sapiens clade” [@wilkins-2021, Section 1. Introduction]

> Human fossils from Florisbad (~260 ka) 31 and Border Cave (~170–80 ka) 30 document the presence of Homo sapiens in southern Africa during the late Middle Pleistocene. [@will-2026-2, Discussion]

> Other early H. sapiens fossils from Florisbad in South Africa (∼260 ka), Omo Kibish (∼195 ka) and Herto (∼160 ka), both in Ethiopia, are morphologically diverse [@scerri-2018, The Morphological Diversity and Spread of the Homo sapiens Clade]

events.title: Neanderthal speciation during MIS 8 in northern Europe

date.marks: Neanderthal speciation, most likely during MIS 8

events.summary: The biological development towards Neanderthal speciation most likely took place during MIS 8 in northern Europe.
events.body: > the biological development towards Neanderthal speciation that most likely took place during MIS 8 [78] , [79] and was established at the beginning of MIS 7, as demonstrated by the braincase morphology of Biache 1 [80] . [@picin-2013, Discussion]

events.title: Florisbad cranium dated, South Africa

date.marks: Date of the Florisbad cranium

events.summary: The partially preserved Florisbad cranium is dated to 259 ka.
events.body:
> the site of Florisbad yielded a partially preserved cranium dated to 259 ka 31 . [@mounier-2019-2, Introduction]

> dated to ca. 260 ka [@meneganzin-2022-2, Section 3.1]

> the complex stratigraphy of the site and the lack of good records on the provenance of the fragments have led some to raise doubts on the contemporaneity of such remains [@meneganzin-2022-2, Section 3.1]

> the site of Florisbad yielded a partially preserved cranium dated to 259 ka 31 . [@mounier-2019, Introduction]

events.title: Florisbad hominin cranium dated to about 259 ka

date.marks: About 259 ka as cited by Herries (2011) from Grün et al. (1996) dating of the cranium; Berger et al. (2017) tabulate 224–294 ka.
date.note: Dates come from direct dating of the Florisbad cranium (Grün et al. 1996); the quoted range is about 259 ± 35 ka.

events.summary: The Florisbad partial cranium, type specimen of Homo helmei, comes from a deposit with Middle Stone Age technology and is dated to about 259 ka, with a published range of 224–294 ka.
events.body:
> the Florisbad hominin skull (the type specimen of Homo helmei [11]) is associated with a “Florisian Land Mammal Age” [@herries-2011-2, Section 1 (Introduction)]

> faunal assemblage and MSA technology and is dated to ~259 ka [@herries-2011-2, Section 1 (Introduction)]

> Florisbad Partial cranium South Africa 224–294 Grün et al. (1996) [@berger-2017, Table of Middle Pleistocene hominin sites]

events.title: Florisbad partial cranium dated by ESR on molar

date.marks: Age of Florisbad cranium, from direct ESR dating of an associated M3

events.summary: A direct ESR assessment on a human third molar associated with the Florisbad cranium yielded an age estimate of 259 ± 35 ka.
events.body:
> a direct electron spin resonance (ESR) assessment on a human M 3 yielded an age estimate of 259 ± 35 ka [@berger-2017-3, Biogeography of subequatorial Africa / Table 1 discussion]

> a direct electron spin resonance (ESR) assessment on a human M 3 yielded an age estimate of 259 ± 35 ka ( Grün et al., 1996 ) [@berger-2017-2, Introduction, Florisbad paragraph]

events.title: Jinniushan hominin skeleton deposited in cave fissure, northeastern China

date.marks: About 260,000 years ago, from ESR and uranium-series dating of animal teeth from Layer 7 (Rosenberg et al. 2006); placement year approximate (about 260 ka).
date.note: Earlier published dates for the specimen were younger but averaged levels higher in the section than the human remains, according to Rosenberg et al.

events.summary: A partial skeleton including a cranium, pelvis and ulna was deposited in Layer 7 of the Jinniushan cave fissure, dated by ESR and U-series on animal teeth to about 260,000 years ago.
events.body:
> Electron-spin resonance and uranium series dating of animal teeth from Layer 7 suggest a date of ≈260,000 years ago [@rosenberg-2006, Background and Dates]

> The Jinniushan specimen was discovered near the town of Yinkou in Liaoning Province in northeastern China [@rosenberg-2006, Background and Dates]

events.title: Hominin remains deposited at Biache-Saint-Vaast, northern France

date.marks: ESR estimate of 253 ka (Yokoyama 1989, cited by Martín-Francés et al. 2022); other estimates: OSL 175 ± 13 ka, ESR/U-series mean ca. 240 ka, one tooth 332 ± 28 ka.
date.note: Dating is disputed: pollen and fauna indicate MIS 7 (240–190 ka); the recent ESR/U-series mean is ca. 240 ka (just outside this period), while the 253 ka ESR age and a 332 ka tooth age fall earlier.

events.summary: Two Middle Pleistocene hominin individuals were found with rich lithic and faunal remains at Biache-Saint-Vaast; dating estimates run from about 175 to 332 ka, with a recent mean of ca. 240 ka.
events.body:
> First dating analyses, including OSL and ESR, provided ages of 175±13 ka (Huxtable and Aikten 1988 ) and 253 + 53/– 37 ka (Yokoyama 1989 ), respectively. [@martin-frances-2022, Introduction]

> provided a mean age of ca. 240 ka (Bahain et al. 2015 ), correlating the human occupation to MIS 7c [@martin-frances-2022, Introduction]

> The hominin remains were associated to a rich lithic and faunal context. [@martin-frances-2022, Introduction]

> the dating result of 332 ± 28 ka obtained for the only tooth of the study that do not show uranium leaching [@martin-frances-2022, Introduction]

events.title: Denisovan mtDNA first appears in Denisova Cave sediments from about 250 ka

date.marks: 'From ~250 ka' per Jacobs et al. (2025), based on optical dating of cave sediments across three chambers and mtDNA from sediment samples; placed at the end of the requested period.
date.note: The authors note some layer ages (e.g. layer 17 in South Chamber) are poorly constrained; the year is a lower bound for the onset of the Denisovan sediment DNA record, not a date for any one event.

events.place: Denisova Cave, Altai, southern Siberia, Russia
events.summary: Sediment DNA and optical dating indicate that the oldest layers containing Denisovan mitochondrial DNA at Denisova Cave accumulated from about 250 ka, with early Middle Palaeolithic stone tools.
aliases: Earliest Denisovan DNA in Denisova Cave sediments
events.body:
> The oldest layers with Denisovan mtDNA accumulated from ~250 ka [@jacobs-2025, Discussion]

> Denisova Cave in southern Siberia is the only site known to have been occupied by Denisovans, Neanderthals and modern humans. [@jacobs-2025, Abstract]

events.title: Earliest MSA-type assemblages at Kathu Pan 1 and Groot Kloof

date.marks: Earliest MSA-type assemblages lacking handaxes, dated to between ~300 and ~200 ka

events.place: Kathu Pan 1 and Groot Kloof, Northern Cape, South Africa
events.summary: The earliest MSA-type assemblages lacking handaxes at Kathu Pan 1 and Groot Kloof are dated between about 300 and 200 ka.
events.body: > The earliest MSA‐type assemblages lacking handaxes are dated to between ~300 and ~200 ka at Kathu Pan 1 and Groot Kloof. [@wilkins-2021, Section 2. Occupation Distribution and Timing]

events.title: Eliye Springs and Guomde fossils in Kenya, 300–200 ka and 270–300 ka

events.summary: Eliye Springs fossils date to ca. 300–200 ka and Guomde fossils to ca. 270–300 ka.
events.body: > Kenya (Eliye Springs, ca. 300–200 ka and Guomde, ca. 270–300 ka) [@meneganzin-2022-2, Section 4.3]

events.title: Eliye Springs skull KNM-ES 11693 dated, Kenya

date.marks: Suggested age of the Eliye Springs skull, based on morphology

events.summary: The Eliye Springs skull KNM-ES 11693 is suggested to be 200–300 ka on the basis of its morphology.
events.body:
> an age of 200–300 ka has been suggested for the nearly complete Eliye Springs skull (KNM-ES 11693 27 ) on the basis of its morphology 28 . [@mounier-2019-2, Introduction]

> an age of 200–300 ka has been suggested for the nearly complete Eliye Springs skull (KNM-ES 11693 27 ) on the basis of its morphology 28 . [@mounier-2019, Introduction]

events.title: Heat-altered fragments at Maastricht-Belvédère, dated to about 250 ka

date.marks: About 250 ka, as stated in a review of Middle Pleistocene fire evidence.
date.note: Interpretation as a combustion structure is disputed.

events.summary: The Middle Palaeolithic site of Maastricht-Belvédère, dated to about 250 ka, yielded concentrations of heat-altered fragments in two groups; one researcher proposes a natural origin for them.
events.body:
> Maastricht-Belvédère (The Netherlands), dated to 250 ka and associated with Middle Paleolithic industry [@stancampiano-2023, Past records of fire within human evolution]

> although Roebroeks 25 proposes a natural origin for such concentrations [@stancampiano-2023, Past records of fire within human evolution]

events.title: Introgression from ancient H. sapiens into Neandertals

date.marks: Introgression occurring 200 to 300 ka, from genetic studies

events.summary: Introgression from ancient H. sapiens into Neandertals is placed at 200 to 300 ka in recent genetic studies.
events.body: > including introgression from ancient H. sapiens into Neandertals occurring 200 to 300 ka [@macdonald-2021, Arguments for a Cultural Explanation]

events.title: Karatau Culture constrained by luminescence ages of PC2

date.marks: Younger limit of the Karatau Culture, from luminescence ages of PC2 and L3

events.summary: A younger limit of about 250 ka for the Karatau Culture is provided by luminescence ages associated with PC2 and L3.
events.body: > a younger limit of ~250 ka 26 , provided by the luminescence ages associated with PC2 (and L3) [@sorensen-2026, Introduction]

events.title: Lake Tana core chronology, Ethiopia

date.marks: base of Lake Tana core from pIR IRSL dating

events.summary: A pIR IRSL-dated core from Lake Tana extends back to about 250 ka and provides a paleoenvironmental framework for hominin dispersal.
events.body:
> which extends back to ∼250 ka [@penkman-2022, 2.2.2. Luminescence in feldspar]

> which extends back to ∼250 ka [@penkman-2022-2, 2.2.2. Luminescence in feldspar]

events.title: LH18 cranium in Ngaloba Beds, Laetoli, Tanzania

date.marks: Age of the LH18 cranium

events.body:
> a 200–300 ka cranium (LH18 29 , 30 ) was discovered in the Ngaloba Beds at Laetoli (Tanzania) [@mounier-2019-2, Introduction]

> a 200–300 ka cranium (LH18 29 , 30 ) was discovered in the Ngaloba Beds at Laetoli (Tanzania) [@mounier-2019, Introduction]

events.title: Oldest recovered hominin mtDNA (Denisovan) in Main Chamber layer 21

date.marks: Start of accumulation of Main Chamber layer 21, from optical dating

events.summary: The oldest hominin mtDNA recovered, identified as Denisovan, comes from Main Chamber layer 21, which began to accumulate 250 ± 44 ka.
events.body: > The oldest hominin mtDNA recovered—identified as Denisovan—originates from a sample in Main Chamber layer 21, which began to accumulate 250 ± 44 ka. [@zavala-2021, Ancient hominin mtDNA]

events.title: Saccopastore Neanderthal skulls dated

date.marks: Age of the Saccopastore skulls

events.summary: The Saccopastore skulls, the oldest Neanderthal specimens for Italy, have an age of about 250 ka.
events.body: > the oldest being the skulls from Saccopastore in Lazio, with an age of ~250 ka [@piccirilli-2025, Section 4 Discussion]

events.title: Deposition of LU1 silty clay at Tam Ngu Hao 2

date.marks: Deposition of the underlying LU1 silty clay, by luminescence dating of block LCC3

events.summary: Luminescence dating of a silty clay block from the lower unit LU1 gave an age of 248 ± 31 kyr.
events.body: > 248 ± 31 kyr (LCC3) for the underlying LU1 silty clay deposit [@demeter-2022, Results, Context and dating]

events.title: Layer 19 accumulated at South Chamber, Denisova Cave

date.marks: Upper limit of accumulation of layer 19, from optical dating (247 ± 39 ka)

events.place: South Chamber, Denisova Cave, Altai, Russia
events.summary: Layer 19 accumulated before 247 ± 39 ka, under cold conditions with open landscapes according to small vertebrate remains.
events.body: > Layer 19 accumulated before 247 ± 39 ka and layer 17 was deposited 202 ± 35 to 167 ± 29 ka. [@jacobs-2025-3, Chronology of sediment deposition]

events.title: Hearth-like combustion structures at Acheulean site of Valdocarros II, Madrid

date.marks: Site dated to MIS 8/7 (~245 kya); occupation range 235–285 kya, with amino-acid racemization ages of 254 ± 47 and 262 ± 07 ka.
date.note: The site is placed between about 285 and 235 ka; 245 ka is the figure used in the title of the study.

events.summary: Lipid biomarkers of incomplete combustion in two hearth-like structures at Valdocarros II are interpreted as evidence of human-controlled fire in an Acheulean context dated to about 245 ka.
events.body:
> Valdocarros II site, one of the largest European Acheulean sites in Spain dated to marine isotopic stage (MIS) 8/7 (~ 245 kya) [@stancampiano-2023, Abstract]

> The presence of combustion byproducts suggests the presence of anthropogenic (controlled) fires at Valdocarros—one of the oldest evidence of fire use in Europe-in association with Acheulean tools and bones. [@stancampiano-2023, Abstract]

> with evidence of human occupancy dating to a range between 235 and 285 kya (MIS 7/8) [@stancampiano-2023, Valdocarros II site]

events.title: Saccopastore Neanderthal skulls assigned to early MIS 7 gravels, Rome

date.marks: Age assigned by correlating Aniene-valley aggradational sediments with sea-level rise at the onset of MIS 7, using published 40Ar/39Ar ages; lowest gravel layer about 245 ka.
date.note: These skulls were formerly attributed to 130,000–80,000 years ago; the sedimentary succession in the area spans 295–220 ka.

events.summary: Chronostratigraphic correlation with sea-level rise assigns the gravel layer holding one Saccopastore Neanderthal skull to about 245 ka, and the uppermost gravel layer to about 220 ka.
events.body:
> we assign ages of 245 ka and 220 ka to the Neanderthal skulls recovered within the lowest and the uppermost gravel layer at Saccopastore, respectively. [@marra-2017, Introduction]

> An age ranging from130,000–80,000 years BP was attributed to these skulls [@marra-2017, Introduction]

events.title: Deposition of ISU2 and Stephanorhinus hundsheimensis survival until MIS 7

date.marks: MIS 7, based on the revised chronology of ISU2

events.summary: Stephanorhinus hundsheimensis is recorded in ISU1 and ISU2, indicating survival in southern Europe until MIS 7.
events.body: > Nevertheless, Stephanorhinus hundsheimensis in Grotta Romanelli indicates that this taxon survived in southern Europe until MIS 7 (ISU2, Fig. 6 ) [@pieruccini-2022, Discussion]

events.title: Spear Horizon deposits dated to MIS 7 by opercula amino acid data

date.marks: MIS 7 age of the Spear Horizon, from intracrystalline amino acid racemization of opercula compared with British and continental comparator sites

events.summary: Amino acid racemization of Bithynia opercula places the Spear Horizon in MIS 7, younger than the Eemian at Neumark-Nord 2 and older than the Holsteinian deposits in Berlin.
events.body:
> an age of MIS 7 is indicated for the Schöningen 13II-4 Spear Horizon, which is substantially younger than all earlier estimates [@hutson-2025-2, Results]

> the Spear Horizon is older than the Eemian deposits at Neumark-Nord 2 [@hutson-2025-2, Results]

events.title: Speleothem growth during Marine Isotope Stages 7, 11 and 15 in central Arabia

date.marks: Growth during Marine Isotope Stages 7, 11 and 15, from U–Th dating

events.summary: Speleothem growth intervals occurred during MIS 7, 11 and 15, coinciding with humid periods in the Negev and southern Arabia.
events.body: > Growth intervals occurred during Marine Isotope Stages (MISs) 7, 11 and 15 coinciding with humid periods also identified in the Negev Desert 20 and in southern Arabia 9 (Extended Data Figs. 8 and 9 ). [@markowska-2025, Recurrent humid episodes]

events.title: Colle Rotondo paleo-surface formed

date.marks: Formation of the paleo-surface, correlated with the MIS 7.5 highstand

events.summary: The Colle Rotondo paleo-surface originated about 240 ka, above sandy deposits of a coastal plain, at the MIS 7.5 highstand.
events.body: > the Colle Rotondo paleo-surface originated circa 240 ka (age of the MIS 7.5 highstand) above the sandy deposits of an alluvial to back-beach coastal plain [@villa-2018, Geomorphology]

events.title: Late Middle Pleistocene deposits at Wadi Lazalim dated by IRSL, southern Tunisia

date.marks: pIRIR290 single-grain feldspar ages: layer 4a 252 ± 23 ka, 4b 232 ± 22 ka, 5 234 ± 22 ka.
date.note: The authors note low resolution; the whole sequence spans about 300–130 ka and layers could belong to MIS 7–8.

events.summary: IRSL ages for layers 4a, 4b and 5 at site 15/1 of the Wadi Lazalim sequence, which has yielded Middle Stone Age human occupation evidence, fall at about 232–252 ka.
events.body:
> the four ages obtained from layers 4a (252 ± 23 ka), 4b (232 ± 22 ka), 5 (234 ± 22 ka) and 9/10 (207 ± 21 ka), are potentially slightly older and could be included in MIS 7–8. [@cancellieri-2022, Results]

> which has yielded evidence for human occupations bracketed between ca. 300–130 ka [@cancellieri-2022, Abstract]

events.place: Thames valley, Salouel and Le Pucheuil, northern France
events.summary: The Levallois method reoccurred at the bridge between MIS 8 and MIS 7 at sites in the Thames valley and northern France.
events.body: > In northern Europe, the Levallois method reoccurred at the bridge between MIS 8 and MIS 7 ( Figure 1B ) in the Thames valley at Yiewsley Area and Creffield Road, Baker’s Hole, Ebbsfleet and the Lion Pit Tramway Cutting [@picin-2013, Chronology of the Emergence of the Levallois in Europe]

events.title: Shala volcano eruption dated 233 ± 22 ka, giving a minimum age for Omo I fossils

date.marks: Age of the proximal deposits of the Shala eruption, 233 ± 22 kyr (40Ar/39Ar dating), a minimum age for the Omo fossils.
date.note: Omo I was previously dated to about 197 kyr from the Nakaa'kire Tuff; the new result is a minimum age and the fossils are older than the eruption.

events.summary: Geochemical correlation links the Kamoya's Hominid Site Tuff, which overlies the Omo I fossil-bearing member of the Omo-Kibish Formation, to a major explosive eruption of Shala volcano, dated 233 ± 22 kyr.

> link the Kamoya’s Hominid Site (KHS) Tuff 9 , which conclusively overlies the member of the Omo-Kibish Formation that contains Omo I, with a major explosive eruption of Shala volcano [@vidal-2022, Abstract]

> By dating the proximal deposits of this eruption, we obtain a new minimum age for the Omo fossils of 233 ± 22 kyr. [@vidal-2022, Abstract]

date.marks: Central date of Cuxton occurrence

events.title: Appearance of Levallois technology in the early MSA of Amanzi Springs by about 230 ka

events.title: Early Neanderthal fossils and tools deposited in Pontnewydd Cave, Wales

events.title: Baume Bonne sequence with Levallois and blades in MIS 8 to 5

events.body: > Assuming constant sedimentation during pollen zone IVa, we can calculate that unit 8 and its associated archaeology accumulated within a maximum period of between 288 ( 34 ) and 455 years ( 33 ) [@kindler-2025, Study area]

events.title: Arrival of Neanderthals in the Neumark-Nord lake landscape

date.marks: Arrival during PAZ III of the Last Interglacial, dated by pollen zones and sedimentation

events.summary: The first documented archaeological presence in the Neumark-Nord basins, marked by a charcoal peak, reflects the arrival of Neanderthals in the wider lake landscape during PAZ III of the Last Interglacial.
events.body:
> The distinctive charcoal peak in the lower part of the Neumark-Nord 2 section correlates with the first documented presence of archaeological finds in the two Neumark-Nord basins, reflecting the arrival of Neanderthals in the wider lake landscape during PAZ III of the Last Interglacial. [@gaudzinski-2023, The Neumark-Nord site complex]

> The distinctive charcoal peak in Unit 6 correlates with the first documented presence of archaeological finds in the two Neumark-Nord basins, reflecting the arrival of Neanderthals in the wider lake landscape [@roebroeks-2021, Results, Vegetation openness at Neumark-Nord]

> With an age of c. 125,000 years, Neumark-Nord provides an early example of a hominin role in vegetation transformation. [@roebroeks-2021, Abstract]

events.title: Bird bone awl in Blombos M3 phase

date.marks: M3 archaeostratigraphic phase at Blombos, dated to about 125 ka or older

events.summary: A bird bone shaped into an awl was recovered from the M3 phase at Blombos, dated to about 125 ka or older.
events.body: > a bird bone that was shaped into an awl was recovered from the M3 archaeostratigraphic phase at Blombos, which has been dated to ∼125 ka ago or older [@hallett-2021, Introduction]

events.title: Bone grease rendering at Neumark-Nord 2/2 before the Upper Paleolithic

date.marks: Grease rendering evidence dated to the Last Interglacial, about 125,000 years ago

events.summary: The NN2/2B assemblage is described as the earliest clear case of intensive grease-rendering documented for the Paleolithic.
events.body:
> The evidence from NN2/2B constitutes the earliest clear case of intensive grease-rendering yet documented for the Paleolithic. [@kindler-2025, DISCUSSION]

> a labor-intensive focus on extracting within-bone nutrients—comparable to behaviors observed among Upper Paleolithic and (sub)recent hunter-gatherer groups—formed a distinct component of the cultural repertoire of hominins in Europe, 125,000 years ago. [@kindler-2025, DISCUSSION]

events.title: Border Cave human remains

date.marks: Border Cave human fossils, dated to about 170–80 ka

events.summary: Human fossils from Border Cave document Homo sapiens, dated to about 170–80 ka.
events.body:
> Border Cave (~170–80 ka) 30 document the presence of Homo sapiens in southern Africa [@will-2026-3, Discussion]

> Border Cave (~170–80 ka) 30 document the presence of Homo sapiens in southern Africa during the late Middle Pleistocene. [@will-2026-2, Discussion]

events.title: Cut-marked remains of 76 rhinos and 40 straight-tusked elephants at Taubach

date.marks: Regional Last Interglacial exploitation evidence at Taubach; date given only as Last Interglacial context

events.summary: The Taubach site contained cut-marked remains of 76 rhinos and 40 straight-tusked elephants, in the Last Interglacial regional record.
events.body: > The last site contained cut-marked remains of 76 rhinos ( 77 ) and 40 straight-tusked elephants ( 76 ). [@kindler-2025, Discussion]

events.title: Earlier dispersals out of Africa during the Last Interglacial

date.marks: Last Interglacial, approximately 125 ka

events.summary: Earlier dispersals out of Africa probably took place during repeated humid episodes, most notably during the Last Interglacial, approximately 125 ka.
events.body: > These dispersals out of Africa probably took place during repeated humid episodes within the Saharo-Arabian arid belt, most notably during the Last Interglacial, approximately 125 ka [@hallett-2025b, Main]

events.title: Early MIS 5e Mediterranean-to-desert expansion of centripetal Levallois at Nahal Aqev

date.marks: oldest occupation of the site, corresponding to MIS 5e

events.summary: The oldest Nahal Aqev occupation, corresponding to MIS 5e, is interpreted as a southern expansion of Middle Paleolithic groups from the Mediterranean woodland.
events.body:
> The oldest occupation of the site, based on luminescence and cryptotephra, corresponds to MIS 5e [@barzilai-2022, Conclusions]

> The emergence of this technology in the Negev during MIS 5e most likely reflects a southern expansion of Middle Paleolithic groups from the Mediterranean woodland [@barzilai-2022, Conclusions]

events.title: Eemian duration in northern Europe

date.marks: Duration of the Eemian interglacial, from varve counting

events.summary: Varve counts from northern German sites give a total duration of about 11 ka for the Eemian.
events.body: > resulting in a total duration of c. 11 ka for the Eemian in northern Europe ( 29 ). [@roebroeks-2021, The Neumark-Nord sites and neighboring basins]

events.title: Lower littoral zone (unit 6.1) formed at Neumark-Nord 1

date.marks: Duration of unit 6.1 lower littoral zone, from sedimentation rates, peat layers and tree ring counts

events.summary: The lower littoral zone of unit 6.1, where most elephant remains were found, existed for about 300 years during a lake regression.
events.body: > Estimates of sedimentation rates, development of peat layers and counting of annual rings in tree stumps indicate that the lower littoral zone (unit 6.1) at Neumark-Nord 1 existed for c. 300 years [@gaudzinski-2023, The Neumark-Nord site complex]

events.title: Nahal Aqev occupation at Unit 11 (lowermost archaeological horizon), central Negev

date.marks: earliest occupation at the site (Unit 11 horizon), from luminescence samples NAQ-8 and NAQ-9 (pIR-IR 250 KF fading-corrected ages)

events.summary: The lowest archaeological horizon, in Unit 11, is the earliest occupation at the site and is dated by luminescence to about 117–134 ka.
events.body:
> samples NAQ-8 and NAQ-9 bracket Unit 11 to between 117 ± 7 ka and 134 ± 7 ka [@barzilai-2022, Luminescence dating (OSL) chronology]

> The lowermost archaeological horizon, and hence the earliest occupation at the site, is embedded within Unit 11. [@barzilai-2022, The site of Nahal Aqev]

events.title: Neanderthal bone grease processing at NN2/2B, Neumark-Nord

date.marks: Neanderthal intensive processing of within-bone nutrients at NN2/2B, dated to about 125,000 years ago

events.summary: Last Interglacial Neanderthals processed a minimum of 172 large mammals at a water's edge site for within-bone nutrients and bone grease.
events.body:
> Neanderthals intensively processed a minimum of 172 large mammals for grease and marrow fat, 125,000 years ago. [@kindler-2025, Abstract]

> Here, we present data on food processing by Last Interglacial Neanderthals, which show that these hunter-gatherers, similar to recent foragers, already focused heavily on the exploitation of within-bone nutrients—and particularly on bone grease—125,000 years ago. [@kindler-2025, INTRODUCTION]

events.title: Neanderthal hunting of straight-tusked elephants in the Last Interglacial, Germany

date.marks: First half of the Last Interglacial, about 125,000 years ago

events.summary: The study states that hunting of straight-tusked elephants at Neumark-Nord 1 was systematic and earliest unambiguous evidence, during the first half of the Last Interglacial.
events.body: > demonstrates that Neanderthals had primary access to fresh carcasses and butchered these in similar ways, involving extensive processing, during the first half of the Last Interglacial [@gaudzinski-2023, Discussion]

events.title: Neanderthal occupation at Neumark-Nord 2, level NN2/2B

date.marks: Deposition during PAZ IV, over 455 years maximum, from sedimentation rates

events.summary: Neanderthals accumulated about 20,000 flint artifacts and 166 large mammals at level NN2/2B during a lake transgression, over a maximum of 455 years.
events.body: > deposited during a time interval of 455 years maximum, as calculated from sedimentation rates during PAZ IV [@gaudzinski-2023, The Neumark-Nord site complex]

events.title: Neanderthal occupation at Neumark-Nord during PAZ III and IV

date.marks: Neanderthal presence during PAZ III and PAZ IV of the Last Interglacial, about 2 ka duration from pollen zone durations

events.summary: Neanderthals were distinctly present at Neumark-Nord during Last Interglacial PAZ III and PAZ IV, a total duration of about 2 ka.
events.body: > At Neumark-Nord, Neanderthals were distinctly present during Last Interglacial PAZ III and PAZ IV, with a total duration of c. 2 ka [@roebroeks-2021, The Neumark-Nord sites and neighboring basins]

events.title: Neanderthal presence at Neumark-Nord for at least 2000 years

date.marks: Neanderthal activity in the Neumark-Nord area over at least 2000 years, Last Interglacial

events.summary: Neanderthals were active in the Neumark-Nord area for at least 2000 years, correlated with a period of vegetation openness.
events.body: > on a broader timescale, Neanderthals were active in this area for at least 2000 years, and their presence is correlated with a period of striking vegetation openness [@kindler-2025, Discussion]

events.title: Neumark-Nord lake landscape occupation during Last Interglacial PAZ III and IV

date.marks: Early Last Interglacial hominin presence, PAZ III and IV, duration about 2850 years

events.summary: Hominins left abundant traces in the lake landscape during the early Last Interglacial, PAZ III and IV, lasting about 2850 years.
events.body: > Hominins left abundant traces of their presence in this lake-dotted landscape, especially in the early parts of the Last Interglacial, i.e., during PAZ III and PAZ IV, with a total duration of ~2850 years. [@kindler-2025, Study area]

events.title: Pre-Carpinus oak-dominated occupation at Rabutz

date.marks: Hominin activity in the pre-Carpinus oak-dominated phase of the Last Interglacial at Rabutz

events.summary: Early 20th-century studies showed hominins were repeatedly active at Rabutz in a pre-Carpinus, oak-dominated phase of the Last Interglacial over several hundred years.
events.body: > demonstrated that hominins were repeatedly active there in a pre- Carpinus , oak-dominated phase of the Last Interglacial in various seasons and probably over a period of several hundreds of years. [@roebroeks-2021, Results, Comparison with other Last Interglacial sites]

events.title: Straight-tusked elephant hunting and butchering at Neumark-Nord 1, Germany

date.marks: Age of the Last Interglacial lake deposits at Neumark-Nord 1, about 125,000 years ago

events.summary: Neanderthals hunted and extensively butchered straight-tusked elephants at the Neumark-Nord 1 lake basin during the Last Interglacial, about 125,000 years ago.
events.body:
> Our archaeozoological study of the largest P. antiquus assemblage known, excavated from 125,000-year-old lake deposits in Germany, shows that hunting of elephants weighing up to 13 metric tons was part of the cultural repertoire [@gaudzinski-2023, Abstract]

> With an age of c. 125,000 years, Neumark-Nord provides a very early example of a hominin role in local-scale vegetation transformation [@gaudzinski-2023, The Neumark-Nord site complex]

events.title: Tidal notch tn3 at 5.5 m a.s.l. correlated with MIS 5e

date.marks: Last Interglacial marine highstand (MIS 5e), inferred from elevation and regional correlation

events.summary: The marine terrace linked to tidal notch tn3 at 5.5 m a.s.l. is correlated with MIS 5e highstand.
events.body: > The marine terrace linked to the tn3 located at 5.5 m a.s.l. in front of the cave entrance [@pieruccini-2022, Discussion]

events.title: Hominin presence in Carpinus phase at Neumark-Nord

date.marks: Ephemeral hominin presence in the Carpinus phase (PAZ V) of the Last Interglacial, undated beyond pollen zone

events.summary: More ephemeral hominin traces in the lake landscape date to the Carpinus (hornbeam) phase, PAZ V.
events.body: > Traces of a more ephemeral hominin presence in this lake landscape date to the Carpinus (hornbeam) phase (PAZ V), characterized here by a closed-canopy forest vegetation. [@kindler-2025, Study area]

events.title: Open vegetation phase at Neumark-Nord (PAZ IV)

date.marks: Open vegetation during PAZ IV of the Last Interglacial, duration estimated from pollen zone durations

events.summary: The landscape stayed open for the whole of PAZ IV, an estimated duration of about 2.2 ka, until closed Carpinus forests developed in PAZ V.
events.body: > The landscape stayed open for the whole of PAZ IV, with an estimated duration of c. 2.2 ka ( 29 ), until the Carpinus phase (PAZ V), when the forests closed. [@roebroeks-2021, Results, Vegetation openness at Neumark-Nord]

events.title: Stone tools deposited at Buhais Rockshelter, AH III (Middle Palaeolithic)

date.marks: Deposition of AH III, dated by OSL on two samples from GH 3 (mean 124 ± 6 ka)

events.place: Buhais Rockshelter, Emirate of Sharjah, UAE
events.summary: The oldest archaeological horizon AH III, a Middle Palaeolithic flake assemblage in GH 3, is dated to about 124 ka.
events.body:
> Two OSL samples from this layer yield a mean age of 124 ka ± 6 ka (Buhais 3: 123 ± 10 ka; Buhais 7: 125 ± 9 ka). [@bretzke-2026, Site stratigraphy]

> contains the oldest archaeological horizon AH III [@bretzke-2026, Site stratigraphy]

events.title: Central Sahara humid corridor during Last Interglacial

date.marks: Humid corridors through central Sahara, from geochemical data and fossil river channels

events.summary: Humid corridors existed through the central Sahara during the Last Interglacial, about 130–117 kya, possibly serving as a dispersal route.
events.body: > humid corridors existed through the central Sahara during the Last Interglacial (specifically in the time range of 130–117 kya) [@beyin-2011, 3.1. The Northern Route]

events.title: Eemian Interglacial, last interglacial before the present

date.marks: Eemian Interglacial (MIS 5e), from the cited chronology

events.summary: The Eemian Interglacial is dated to between about 130 and 115 ka, the last interglacial before the present day.
events.body: > The Eemian Interglacial was the last interglacial to occur prior to the present day, dated to between ~130–115 ka [@nelson-2025, 4.1.1 Eemian and Weichselian]

events.title: Closed forest phase with Carpinus at Neumark-Nord (PAZ V)

date.marks: Carpinus phase (PAZ V) of the Last Interglacial, about 4 ka duration from pollen zone durations

events.summary: The Carpinus (hornbeam) phase PAZ V was a closed forest phase of about 4 ka, with only ephemeral hominin presence documented.
events.body:
> PAZ V concerns a closed forest dominated by Carpinus (hornbeam). [@roebroeks-2021, Results, Vegetation openness at Neumark-Nord]

> for this c. 4-ka-long closed-forest phase, only an ephemeral hominin presence has been documented at Neumark-Nord [@roebroeks-2021, Results, Vegetation openness at Neumark-Nord]

events.title: Lichtenberg Li-BPa horizons dated within the Eemian

date.marks: Eemian horizons in the Li-BPa borehole, from a Bayesian age-depth model using quartz OSL and pIRIR ages

events.place: Lichtenberg Li-BPa borehole, Lower Saxony, Germany
events.summary: The deeper Lichtenberg horizon is placed in the earliest part of the Eemian at about 126.5–128 ka, and the shallower one in its later part at about 118–119 ka.
events.body: > The Bayesian age-depth model places the deeper of the two horizons in the earliest part (ca. 126.5 to 128 ± 8.6 ka) and the shallower horizon in the later part of the interglacial (ca. 118 to 119 ± 8.2 ka). [@nelson-2025, 4.1.1 Eemian and Weichselian]

events.title: Speleothem deposition in Negev caves between 126 and 118 ka

date.marks: limited speleothem deposition in the Ashalim, Mizpe Ramon and Ma'aleh HaMeishar caves

events.place: Ashalim, Mizpe Ramon and Ma'aleh HaMeishar caves, Negev, Israel
events.summary: Limited speleothem deposition in three Negev caves is dated to between 126 and 118 ka.
events.body: > This may correspond to the limited deposition of speleothems between 126 and 118 ka in the Ashalim, Mizpe Ramon and Ma'aleh HaMeishar caves [@barzilai-2022, Discussion]

events.title: Heated flint artifacts at find level NN2/2B, Neumark-Nord 2

date.marks: Heated flint artifacts from find level NN2/2B, dated by thermoluminescence

events.summary: Thermoluminescence dating of heated flint artifacts from find level NN2/2B gives a weighted mean age of 121 ± 5 ka.
events.body: > thermoluminescence dating of heated flint artifacts from find level NN2/2B with a weighted mean age of 121 ± 5 ka [@roebroeks-2021, The Neumark-Nord sites and neighboring basins]

events.title: Baume Flandin Levallois blade débitage dated to MIS 5e

date.marks: Blade débitage at Baume Flandin, dated to MIS 5e

events.place: Baume Flandin, near Payre, Rhône Valley
events.summary: Baume Flandin, close to Payre, is dated to MIS 5e and shows blade débitage by a Levallois concept.
events.body: > This is also the case for Baume Flandin, close to Payre and dated to the MIS 5e [@carmignani-2017, Payre and the Bau de l'Aubesier in the MIS 9–7 European context]

events.title: Burnt flints dated at Tinshemet Cave Terrace units B1b and C, earlier human presence

date.marks: Earlier human presence at the Terrace (bottom of Unit B1b and Unit C), from thermoluminescence dating of burnt flints (mean 120.4 ± 14 ka)
date.note: Four TL samples give older ages than the rest of the sequence, which the authors interpret as possibly an earlier presence.

events.summary: Thermoluminescence ages of burnt flints from the bottom of Unit B1b and Unit C suggest an earlier human presence at the site, with values around 117 to 173 ka.
events.body:
> These four samples indicate that the bottom of Unit B1b and Unit C may represent an earlier human presence at the site. [@zaidner-2025, Thermoluminescence dating]

> two samples from Unit C, which give ages of 124 ± 14 and 117 ± 14 ka (mean age, 120.4 ± 14 ka) [@zaidner-2025, Thermoluminescence dating]

events.title: Denisovan-to-Neanderthal habitat shift in the Altai

date.marks: Habitat simulations for Denisovans and Neanderthals, 1000-year timesteps

events.summary: Potentially suitable habitat decreased for Denisovans and increased for Neanderthals between about 130 and 110 ka, based on simulations.
events.body: > These timings match the decrease in potentially suitable Altai habitat for Denisovans and increase for Neanderthals between ~130 and ~110 ka [@jacobs-2025-3, Discussion]

events.title: Earliest bone tools for fur and leather working at Contrebandiers Cave

date.marks: Earliest bone tools and carnivore skinning marks at the site, from luminescence dating of the oldest layers

events.summary: Bone tools likely used for leather and fur working are dated to as early as about 120 ka at Contrebandiers Cave.
events.body: > we present evidence for fur removal found on carnivore bones dated to as early as 120 ka ago at Contrebandiers Cave in Morocco [@hallett-2021, Introduction]

events.title: Ganqian Cave hominin fossils, South China

date.marks: Age range of hominin fossils from Ganqian Cave

events.place: Ganqian Cave, Tubo, Liujiang, Guangxi, South China
events.summary: Hominin fossils tentatively attributed to H. sapiens at Ganqian Cave are dated to about 140 to 100 ka.
events.body: > Ganqian Cave (140 to 100 ka) ( 41 ) [@ao-2024, Climatic Influence on Initial AMH Dispersal to East Asia]

events.title: Hunting and hide use by early occupants of Contrebandiers Cave

date.marks: Occupation of Contrebandiers Cave by about 120 ka

events.summary: By about 120 ka, people occupied Contrebandiers Cave, hunting 67 species of vertebrate animals for food and hides.
events.body: > By ∼120 ka ago in North Africa, people occupied Contrebandiers Cave, hunting 67 species of vertebrate animals [@hallett-2021, Discussion]

events.title: Neanderthal speciation postdated to MIS 6, Saccopastore crania (MIS 5)

date.marks: Saccopastore early Neanderthal crania, MIS 5

events.summary: The speciation event towards Homo neanderthalensis is postdated to MIS 6, as shown by the crania of two early Neanderthals from Saccopastore dated to MIS 5.
events.body: > the speciation event towards Homo neanderthalensis is postdated to MIS 6, as demonstrated by the crania of the two early Neanderthals from Saccopastore (MIS 5) [81] [@picin-2013, Discussion]

events.title: Neumark Nord II Blake Event marker

date.marks: Blake Event, dated to 0.12 Ma

events.summary: Neumark Nord II is attributed to the Eemian partly on evidence for the Blake Event dated to 0.12 Ma.
events.body: > evidence for the Blake Event (0.12 Ma; Sier et al ., 2011 ,2015 ). [@nelson-2025, 4.1.1 Eemian and Weichselian]

events.title: Pierced shell beads indicate cord knowledge

date.marks: Pierced shell beads, by 120 000 years ago

events.summary: Pierced shell beads by 120 000 years ago indicate knowledge of twine or leather cord.
events.body: > By 120 000 years ago, pierced shell beads [ 141 ] indicate a knowledge of twine or leather cord [@gowlett-2016, 6. Fire origins in the archaeological record]

events.title: Scladina and Hohlenstein-Stadel Neanderthals dated to about 120 ka

date.marks: Age of the Scladina and Hohlenstein-Stadel mtDNA, from molecular dating

events.summary: The Scladina and Hohlenstein-Stadel Neanderthals are dated to about 120 ka by molecular dating.
events.body: > contemporaneous Neanderthals of Scladina and Hohlenstein-Stadel dated to ~ 120 ka (95% HPDI:, ~ 82–161 ka, and 95% HPDI: ~ 69–187 ka, respectively; Table S8 ). [@picin-2020, Discussion]

events.title: Stone heating at Pinnacle Point

date.marks: Stone warming, before 120 000 years ago

events.summary: Before 120 000 years ago at Pinnacle Point, stone was being warmed to improve its working qualities.
events.body: > Before this date at Pinnacle Point in South Africa, stone was being warmed to improve its working qualities [@gowlett-2016, 6. Fire origins in the archaeological record]

events.title: Langebaan footprints, South Africa

date.marks: Trackway of three footprints in epirelief

events.summary: A trackway of three footprints at Langebaan was dated to about 117 ka.
events.body: > A trackway comprising three footprints in epirelief was described, and dated to ~ 117 ka 44 [@decarvalho-2025, Review of the coastal hominin track records]

events.title: Oldest MSA bone tools in Layers 5 and 6, Central Excavation Area

date.marks: Earliest bone tools in Layers 5 and 6 of the CEA, from grand weighted mean OSL age

events.place: Contrebandiers Cave, central excavation area, Morocco
events.summary: The earliest occurrence of bone tools in the central excavation area is dated by a weighted mean OSL age of 116.1 ± 2.9 ka.
events.body: > The weighted mean OSL age of 116.1 ± 2.9 ka, therefore, best constrains the age of the oldest bone tools found in Layers 5 and 6 in the CEA [@hallett-2021, Checking the reliability of the OSL chronology]

events.title: Earliest hafted tools in Xigou assemblage, Eastern Asia

date.marks: Xigou occupation dated by ReOSL luminescence to about 160–72 ka

events.summary: Hafted tools from Xigou, dated to about 160–72 thousand years ago, are described as the earliest composite tools known in Eastern Asia.
events.body:
> The identification of the hafted tools provides the earliest evidence for composite tools in Eastern Asia, to our knowledge. [@yue-2026, Abstract]

> In particular, hafting technology, demonstrated by technological and use-wear approaches from Xigou, to our knowledge, provides the earliest known evidence of this kind for stone tool assemblages in Eastern Asia. [@yue-2026, Discussion: Early technological innovations from the Middle to Late Pleistocene in China]

events.title: Eemian sediments absent at Stajnia Cave

date.marks: Eemian interglacial period (MIS 5e)

events.summary: Eemian sediments (123–109 ka) are absent in Stajnia Cave.
events.body: > since Eemian sediments (123–109 ka) are absent in the cave [@picin-2020, Discussion]

events.title: Elephant and camel footprints at Alathar paleolake

date.marks: Animal tracks in the footprint-bearing surface, bracketed by OSL ages

events.place: Alathar paleolake, western Nefud Desert, Saudi Arabia
events.summary: Elephant and camel tracks document herds moving through the landscape around the lake during the last interglacial.
events.body: > Elephant ( n = 43) and camel ( n = 107) footprints are most abundant and document herds (i.e., adults and juveniles) moving through the landscape [@stewart-2020, Fossil and footprint evidence]

events.title: Genetic age of Stajnia S5000 mtDNA genome

date.marks: Divergence/age of the S5000 mtDNA genome, from molecular branch shortening in the mtDNA tree

events.summary: The mtDNA genome of Stajnia S5000 dates to about 116 ka by molecular branch length, with a 95% HPDI of 83–152 ka.
events.body: > we estimated that the mtDNA genome of Stajnia S5000 dates to ~ 116 ka according to the branch length of the mtDNA tree, albeit with large confidence intervals (95% HPDI: 83,101–152,515 years ago). [@picin-2020, Results]

events.title: Hominin footprints at Alathar, probably Homo sapiens

date.marks: Hominin footprints dated by the OSL age bracket of the footprint-bearing unit

events.place: Alathar paleolake, western Nefud Desert, Saudi Arabia
events.summary: Seven hominin footprints were confidently identified at Alathar, attributed to H. sapiens and dated within the last interglacial.
events.body: > Seven hominin footprints were confidently identified, and given the fossil and archeological evidence for the spread of H. sapiens into the Levant and Arabia during MIS 5 [@stewart-2020, Fossil and footprint evidence]

events.title: Human and animal footprints deposited at Alathar paleolake, western Nefud Desert

date.marks: Footprints on the top of unit 4b, bracketed by OSL samples from units 2 and 5, dated by optically stimulated luminescence

events.place: Alathar paleolake, western Nefud Desert, Saudi Arabia
events.summary: Hominin and non-hominin mammal footprints were made on the surface of the Alathar lake deposit, bracketed by OSL ages of about 121 and 112 ka.
events.body: > Samples for optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating were taken from sediments directly below (unit 2; PD61) and above (unit 5; PD62) the footprint-bearing unit and yielded ages of 121 ± 11 and 112 ± 10 ka, respectively, effectively bracketing the age of the prints [@stewart-2020, Geology and geochronology]

events.title: Stalagmite beneath the Sant'Agostino deposit

date.marks: Stalagmite beneath the deposit, dated by U-series

events.summary: The Sant'Agostino deposit rests on a stalagmite dated by U-series to 112 ± 14 ka and 120 ± 15 ka.
events.body: > The deposit rests on a stalagmite, dated by U-series to 112 ± 14 ka and 120 ± 15 ka [ 97 ]. [@degano-2019, Dating]

events.title: Stone tool occupation at Xigou, Danjiangkou Reservoir Region, central China (Layers 2–5)

date.marks: Cultural horizons (Layers 2–5) of the Xigou sequence, dated by quartz ReOSL luminescence

events.place: Xigou, Danjiangkou Reservoir Region, Henan Province, central China
events.summary: Cultural horizons Layers 2–5 at Xigou, with lithic assemblages of core-on-flake, discoid and hafted tools, date between about 160 and 72 thousand years ago.
events.body:
> The ReOSL chronology dates the cultural horizons (Layers 2–5) between ~160 and 72 ka. [@yue-2026, Results: Site setting, stratigraphy, and ages]

> the bottom of the sediment column dates to 285.4 ± 15.7 ka and Layers 2–6, ranging in depth from 2.65 to 0.75 m, accumulated between 191.6 ± 13.3 to 71.9 ± 4.0 ka [@yue-2026, Results: Site setting, stratigraphy, and ages]

events.title: Deposition of Neumark-Nord 2 infill and Early Weichselian loess

date.marks: End of the interglacial sequence at Neumark-Nord, with Early Weichselian loess deposits

events.summary: The Neumark-Nord 2 interglacial sequence ends with Early Weichselian loess deposits.
events.body: > At both basins, the interglacial sequence ends with Early Weichselian loess deposits. [@roebroeks-2021, The Neumark-Nord sites and neighboring basins]

events.title: Earliest pressure flakers at Lingjing, China

date.marks: Earliest pressure flakers at Lingjing

events.summary: The earliest pressure flakers are dated to about 125–105 ka at Lingjing, China.
events.body: > The earliest pressure flakers date to ∼125–105 ka ago at Lingjing, China [@hallett-2021, Results]

events.title: Middle Paleolithic occupations at Nahal Aqev, MIS 5e to MIS 5d

date.marks: span of Middle Paleolithic occupations, from luminescence and cryptotephra chronology

events.summary: The luminescence and cryptotephra chronology dates the Middle Paleolithic occupations at the site from MIS 5e to MIS 5d.
